As for the third argument, choice and intention bring about the beginning of an action, while their continuation goes with the action's continuation. If intention and choice continue, they can continue to direct an action as well. To claim this is impossible simply assumes what is in question.

As for the fourth argument, builders and writers cause bodies to move and change place. They are not the causes that preserve a building's shape, keep things in place, or make them last. Other, nearer or more distant causes do that. I will explain this in its proper place.

Chapter 39 — Why every event in time depends on an unbroken circular motion

Know675 that a complete cause cannot come before or after its effect in time. So the immediate causes of events must themselves come into being. If they had always existed, their effects would have always existed too. Whenever a cause exists while its effect does not, the effect is possible in relation to that cause: what is impossible in itself cannot be produced by a cause. So when the effect does come into being, something else must tip the balance toward its existence rather than its nonexistence. That something also needs a cause, and the same question arises again, until we reach what makes the effect necessary and brings it into being.

The immediate cause of an event, or at least one part of its cause, must therefore come into being along with it. We can ask the same question about that new cause. This leads either to an endless chain or to an event whose very nature is to change and come into being, such as motion, or a nature that renews itself.676 But a nature that comes and goes, whose absence belongs to an earlier time and motion, must be preceded by another nature that keeps its time. This time-keeping nature has two sides. One is known to God: His eternal knowledge and the form of His decree, which is not part of the created world. The other belongs to the created world and comes into being anew each day.

The philosophers accepted an endless chain because they had not found this principle. They said the chain must either exist all at once or be arranged so that one thing comes before another. The first option is impossible, as we have already shown, so they chose the second. But then the events in the chain must either be separate instants or unfold over time. If they are separate instants, they must follow one another without end. That is impossible. And even if it were possible, each instant would be separate from the next, so the earlier instant would not have to end in the later one. It could not be the cause of the later instant, contrary to what they assumed. If the events unfold over time, they are motion.

Here is the point. When something new arises in matter—for example, a human form in semen—the cause gains a relation to that matter that it did not have before. The matter must move and change so that what was far from receiving the form comes closer. The semen undergoes a connected series of changes. Its powers and conditions shift until it becomes suited to receive that form from its active cause.

To explain this, a cause may either prepare something or bring about its effect. A preparing cause may come before the effect because it does not produce the effect itself. It only brings the recipient close to the point where the acting cause can produce it. The acting cause, by contrast, must be present with its effect. Preparation consists of a real process of change, linked step by step: each new state can arise only after the previous one has passed away.

Consider a heavy body falling. It does not reach any point along its path without becoming ready to move from there to the next point. Reaching each point prepares it for the next part of its fall. Its weight is what moves it. But until the body has reached a given point, its weight cannot move it from there. Once it reaches that point, its weight can move it onward. The earlier motion brings the body closer to the next effect; this is what philosophers mean when they say that motion brings causes closer to their effects.

The same thing happens when someone walks through a dark place by the light of a lamp. As the person steps onto a patch of ground lit by the lamp, the light falls on the next patch, which the person can then reach. The lamp directly causes the light on each patch; walking prepares the next patch to be reached. Likewise, someone who intends to make a pilgrimage has one general aim that gives rise to a sequence of smaller intentions. Reaching each point along the way makes it possible to form the next intention and move toward the next point. The general aim causes these smaller intentions and the movements that follow them, and remains present throughout.

With this in mind, we can see that one acting cause remains present with all the distinct effects that arise one after another. This is what makes it a cause and gives rise to its effects. The individual events have their own earlier and later order, but that order is part of their very nature; no cause makes one event earlier or another later. The cause brings about the events themselves, not the fact that one comes first and another comes after. The stages of a falling body's path are like the forms taken by gravity; the patches of light on the ground are like the forms taken by the lamp's light; and the smaller intentions are like the forms taken by the single general aim.

In the same way, each changing natural kind has an eternal cause that gives rise to its changing forms. But the cause's effect on each particular thing comes at its proper time, when matter has become ready and strongly disposed to receive it. This readiness arises through motion and change, and through the distinct forms that follow one another in matter: the earlier forms prepare matter to receive the later ones.

Nothing, then, can come into being without earlier events linked to it. There must be an unending sequence of events, each following another, with no first event. There must also be something that can continue to renew itself without interruption, so that time itself does not stop. This must be a body with one nature that keeps changing without a break and another aspect that remains in God's knowledge. Among bodily substances, the simple body created directly by God can renew itself without interruption. Among bodily qualities, the circular motion can continue without end; other motions and changes stop at a boundary that separates them from what follows.

You will learn that what causes this motion is not a body. It longs without end for the divine realm. From God it begins, and to God it returns, riding a celestial ship: “In the name of God be its course and its anchorage.”

Then comes the second section of the First Journey, followed by the third, which begins with Stage Seven. This completes the First Journey of The Transcendent Wisdom in the Four Intellectual Journeys, by the philosopher of the East, the wonder of his age, the divine sage Mulla Sadra (Ṣadr al-Dīn Muḥammad al-Shīrāzī)—may God bless his pure soul. We praise God for this success and ask Him to help us publish the remaining parts of the book soon. He is the Guardian, the Almighty. We also owe deep thanks to all the learned people and printing-house staff who helped us print and correct the book. We pray that God grant them success and happiness in both worlds. Amen, Lord of all worlds.

Publisher (Qom Press): Despite our great effort to produce this book without serious errors, circumstances—from the printer to the proofreader—combined to leave this page of corrections at the end. Perhaps a few minor errors escaped our notice. Readers are asked to correct the book using this table before they begin reading.

Notes

  1. Scholars use this account of essence, but it is not a strict definition; it explains the word. The concept of essence is not one of the external essences placed under the ten broad categories used to classify things. It is a general feature that can be said of all the categories and their kinds. This definition also differs from the later one, “that by which a thing is what it is.” Here, saying that essence answers “What is it?” shows that the thing being defined is a concept that can exist in the mind. Of things outside the mind, this applies to their essence, not to their existence or their being outside the mind. The second wording can apply to both a thing’s essence and its existence, so it is broader. What, then, does the first definition mean? From the arguments in the earlier discussion of existence, we learned that external realities—or most of them—have two connected aspects: existence, which cannot enter the mind, and essence, which is united with external existence in the world and with mental existence in the mind. There is no third aspect. So concepts that describe external things as existing, but do not directly fit those things, are not essences. They are ideas made by the mind and exist only there. Outside the mind there are only existence and the essences that exist through it. Other ideas formed by the mind are not present there as ideas. When we say, literally, “it is,” we mean what is present outside the mind: its real existence and the essence that expresses what it is. Other concepts, even features that follow from essences—such as the evenness of four and the oddness of three—are made by the mind and are not present outside as concepts, though they may have examples there. Essence, as what a thing is, therefore matches the thing’s real identity. If we ask what an intelligible thing is, we seek a concept identical with its external identity, one that cannot be separated from it; only essence answers. Thus essence is what answers “What is it?” — ط مد

    ↩

  2. A thing becomes particular when features foreign to its essence are added to it, so particularity belongs to it only by accident. The nature itself is universal. Particularity in the sense of being an individual, however, belongs to actual existence. Essence, both in itself and as the answer to “What is it?”, is universal, but universality is a feature outside it that necessarily belongs to it in the mind. In itself it is neither universal nor particular. So there is no conflict between saying that essence is a universal concept and saying that it is not, in itself, either universal or particular. — ط مد

    ↩

This is self-evident. One might object that the same form of denial also applies to concepts that are not essences. The answer is that these judgments properly belong to essence; they apply to other concepts only by extension, because those concepts are drawn from essences in the mind. This also answers a related objection: universality and particularity apply to non-essential concepts too, but that does not make them essential features of those concepts. — ط مد

  15. The question is about essence considered in itself. This differs from a question that offers a true contradictory pair: there, we answer with one side, the negative one. The confusion does not arise in that case, because one question asks whether essence is described under the condition of being considered in itself, while the other denies that description. One might object that both questions concern essence under this same condition, so the same confusion should arise. The reply is that we do not say, “Essence in itself is not this”; we say, “Essence is not, when considered in itself, this.” That is another reason for putting the denial before the qualification: the level applies to the thing whose feature is denied, not to the denial itself. The commentator quotes Avicenna’s The Healing, where he distinguishes a question offering one affirmative and one negative answer from a question offering two affirmative descriptions that seem to form an either-or. In the first case, the answer must use the denial before the qualification, as in the main text. In the second, we do not have to choose: the essence may be free of both descriptions when considered in itself.   24. External existence has effects in the world, so it cannot enter the mind in that form. What we learn about an object through the mind is an image without those effects. The author means this kind of direct witnessing. It is less clear how sensation itself could make something particular. A mental image, whether sensory or imagined, does not by itself prevent the mind from applying it to more than one thing. Another judgment is needed, such as that two identical things cannot exist, or that existence makes a thing individual. The image itself does not rule out more than one match, though a sensory or imagined image is narrower than a general idea such as humanity. Sensory awareness may work because sensible features take on a form in the sense organ like the form they have outside. The soul, joined to the body, becomes one with that form, then forms a mental image that matches the object. This connection may explain why the same sensory awareness cannot be shared among the outward senses. Inner awareness, such as knowing one’s own love or hatred, more clearly involves the thing being present to the soul. As for imagined images, it is the mind’s judgment that they represent one external individual that prevents sharing—not the image alone. — ط مد

  34. The statements that a species is its general kind and distinguishing feature are made at the level of what the thing is, with outside features—including actual existence—set aside. They mean, for example, “a human is an animal” and “a human is rational.” They are not claims about an actual person. This does not mean the general kind and the distinguishing feature are the same as each other. Each belongs to the species in a different way. If the feature were already part of the general kind’s definition, the distinction between them would collapse. If the general kind were part of the feature’s definition, explaining it would go on without end. Each is outside the definition of the other. The general kind is the broad side of the species; the feature makes it specific; the species is the complete kind. They are called parts because both appear in its definition. By itself, the general kind does not determine a feature; the distinguishing feature makes the subject definite enough for features to belong to it. It can also have some properties when it is itself an intermediate kind. — ط مد

A general kind is shared by different complete kinds because it is joined to their distinguishing features.   59. One might object that this does not solve the problem: if a thing is simple, how can the mind divide it into parts and draw several meanings from it without merely inventing them? The answer will become clearer in the later discussion of cause and effect, where the author turns to the insights of the mystics. These meanings have distinct forms in the mind, drawn from one thing as the mind becomes aware of fewer or more similarities and differences. In general, there are several views on how the mind forms parts from a simple thing. Al-Sharīf reports them after noting that everyone agrees the parts are distinct in the mind. The first view says they are distinct both in nature and in existence; this view is weak. The second says they are distinct in nature but not in existence, because it treats nature as prior to existence; on this view, the objection disappears. The third says they are one in nature and in existence; this makes the objection harder to answer. The answer is the one already given: the mind takes these meanings in different ways. Mulla Sadra rejects all three views and chooses a fourth, also suggested by al-Sharīf: outside the mind there is only a way of existing. The mind draws essential and nonessential meanings from it according to how many similarities and differences it notices. The author will explain this later. This is also what he means by saying that a distinguishing feature is a way of existing. He singles out the feature because the general kind is absorbed into it, and the kind gets its identity from that feature. — س ره

  60. Someone might object: if the mind does not divide the general kind and its distinguishing feature, they are simply one, so neither can cause the other. But if the mind does divide them, they become matter and form, and then form—not the distinguishing feature—would be the cause. The author points to the answer by calling them two mental parts. There is a third option: they are neither wholly different, as matter and form are, nor wholly one, as they are in the outside world. They have something of both, as the author explained earlier when discussing the different ways a nature can be considered. This resembles the familiar problem of how we can learn something unknown. The answer is that what we seek is not wholly unknown: it is unknown in one respect and known in another. Someone may object that we cannot seek what is unknown or learn what we already know. But we are not seeking two things; we are seeking one thing with two aspects. The mistake comes from treating two ways of considering one thing as if they were two separate things. We can also take the opposite route and speak of causes in the outside world, which is the philosopher’s proper subject: there, the natural distinguishing feature is form, and the natural general kind is matter, so the question does not arise. Another view says the general kind and its feature are one in the world, in nature and in existence; on that view, too, the question disappears. The answer in the main text, however, rests on considering them in ways that are true within reality, as the author explained earlier and will explain again. Mulla Sadra accepts none of these views. He chooses a fourth, also suggested by al-Sharīf: outside the mind there is only a way of existing; the mind draws essential and nonessential meanings from it according to what it sees as shared or distinguishing. This is what he means by saying the distinguishing feature is a way of existing. He singles out the feature because the general kind is absorbed into it, and the specific kind gets its identity from it. — س ره

  61. In real compounds, if we treat the general kind as matter and the distinguishing feature as form, the explanation is fuller: form works with matter as a cause.   66. “Form” can refer to a thing’s kind, its general kind, or its distinguishing feature, especially when the mind turns it into a mental image; in that case, two technical uses overlap. Such discussion concerns things that have forms in the world. This is what Avicenna means when he says that form can refer to a thing’s kind, general kind, distinguishing feature, or all of them together. The form that gives matter its reality is bodily form, and the matter is first matter. The form that shapes a thing into a natural kind is its specific form; the thing receiving it is matter already made into a body. The author has not listed every use of “form,” though Avicenna does so near the end of his discussion of natural bodies, gathering them under one meaning: what makes a thing actually be what it is. The same applies to the parts of things, and to terms such as priority, potential, and possibility. Or perhaps the author means that these uses share a meaning, rather than being unrelated uses of the same word. Avicenna says in The Healing that form can mean any actual meaning fit to be understood, including separate intelligences; any state or activity in one thing or in a compound, including motion and qualities; what makes matter actual; what completes matter without making it what it is, such as health or a natural tendency toward it; a special shape made in matter by craft; or a thing’s kind, general kind, distinguishing feature, or all of these. He adds that the whole can also serve as the form of its parts. — س ره

  67. The wording may seem contradictory because “its matter” suggests that matter is part of the thing’s essence. The phrase “what bears its form” resolves this: the bearer lies outside the form it bears. — س ره

  73.   78. One might object: If this is so, then what makes a thing what it is must be its distinguishing feature. The general kind is absorbed into that feature, as will be explained later. The answer is that the distinguishing feature here is not an actual thing that can absorb something else. In this case the relation is the reverse. This is like an exception to the rule, not because the rule is being narrowed, but because the case does not fall under it: when a distinguishing feature or form is fully actual, the general kind is absorbed into it, and the thing is what it is through that form. Matter, by contrast, has no form or distinguishing feature of its own.   79. In other words, nothing in the outside world corresponds to the general concept as such; that concept cannot itself be included in “rational.” A particular thing does exist, but it is a specific substance or a specific accident, such as a quality.   80. There is a deep point here. The general kind is a feature that necessarily accompanies the true distinguishing feature, while the true distinguishing feature is the complete reality of a thing: a thing is what it is through that feature and no other. Everything else lies outside its essential reality. It is said that the final definition in a chain of definitions is the same as the middle term in a proof. The true distinguishing feature is the reality of the true cause. God, exalted be He, is the highest completion of all things. Understand this. — ن ره

  81. Once it is established that all distinguishing features—from the first feature in the most basic composition to the last feature in any composite, and all forms from the first to the last—are existence and have no substantial or accidental essence of their own, it follows that the whole world is existence. This is a lofty idea, understood by a mature philosopher. The claim may seem to conflict with familiar principles: that a distinguishing feature is part of an essence, helps compose it, is one of the five predicables, and can be used with a general kind to define a nature. But the conflict is only apparent. The author’s view rests on the fourth account of mental composition discussed earlier. If a distinguishing feature is understood as a mode of existence, as the author holds, these principles do not contradict it. If instead it is understood as a simple essence, as others hold, then the instruction to keep it from outsiders may reflect their failure to see how a possible essence used as a distinguishing feature can be neither a substance nor a quality, even though the argument leads to this conclusion. A distinguishing feature of a substance is not itself a substance in the essential sense in which a general kind is; otherwise it would itself be composite. The same applies to distinguishing features of qualities: they do not belong essentially to the general category of quality, and likewise for the other categories. Saying that every possible essence is either a substance or a quality requires only that it be classified in some way, not that the classification be essential. — س ره

  82. The author’s argument is not conclusive. Although general kind and distinguishing feature correspond to external matter and form in a substance, and although the mind considers the general kind and distinguishing feature as distinct, that does not mean the mental relation must hold in the outside world. Relations can differ depending on whether we consider something in the mind or outside it. For example, whether a statement can be affirmed varies with the standpoint. A final form can exist without the earlier matter and forms, and a kind can exist without its matter once its form is separate. This is possible in the outside world, but not if we look only at mental parts. There are other cases where the two standpoints yield different judgments. The argument, then, does not establish its conclusion, even though the conclusion may be true for another reason. — ط مد

  83. The author has not said here that these forms are existence, but he has already said that distinguishing features in general are modes of existence. One might object that not being a substance or quality does not prove that something is existence: unity, a point, and motion, for example, may be outside the categories without being existence. The answer is that a thing must be either existence or an essence. If it is not an essence, it is existence. Existence is either unbounded and infinitely intense—God—or a particular mode of existence, which is possible existence. Nothing can be neither existence nor essence. Unity is existence; a point is a privation; and, as the author argues through substantial motion, motion is a mode of existence in the natural world. This is the author’s position: distinguishing features are existence, not essences, because essences are mental abstractions and cannot make a general kind actual. Others may instead take these features to be simple essences, neither substances nor qualities in themselves, though they can be called substances or qualities in a secondary sense. The author appears to follow this latter view in the next argument: he says the soul is a substance when considered in itself, but not when considered as the body’s form. — س ره

That reading is mistaken: these are mental concepts drawn from essences, not essences in their own right. If they were essences, they would themselves have existence, and existence would then have another existence. That is clearly wrong. The better reading is the one given above, though it takes some effort to reconcile it with the author’s later examples of existence and immediate awareness. Those examples may be only comparisons. — ط مد

  85. The true distinguishing feature, which is real existence, is neither substance nor quality. As explained earlier, all things perish and fade in the one true reality of existence. All distinct forms are levels of the reality of existence, and their appearance as separate things is only figurative and dependent. He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden; all things are mirrors of His manifestation, and as mirrors they vanish in what is reflected in them. Nothing stands between Him and you but your own self. Let go of what occupies you, and what truly matters will be revealed. — ن ره

  86. How could the existence of a separate substance depend on a particular readiness in matter at a particular time, when it is equally related to every time and separate from matter? But a separate reality is distinct in its essence from matter and bodies. How, then, could it be a state of matter? This objection applies to anyone who holds that the soul begins to exist but is immaterial, including Mulla Sadra, who says that it becomes spiritual in its later life. It does not apply to Platonists who hold that the soul has always existed. The details will come in the discussion of the soul, God willing. — س ره

  87. That is, not in itself. The body may call for it indirectly, and this allows the soul’s immaterial essence to begin to exist in time.   88. The point is not that the source of the soul’s existence here and in time is the bodily existence itself. First, the soul’s bodily existence is its active, material existence—not its sacred essence. As the Persian verse says: “You are too great to appear in this little mirror.” Second, if matter’s readiness were not required here, and divine generosity alone were enough, then a rational soul would have been given even to an ant. The point is that the body calls for something that acts through matter, and that this active aspect is connected to its source and inner reality: the Active Intellect, whose existence comes directly from divine generosity and from the possibility in its own essence. Intellects exist through their own essential possibility, without a need for matter’s readiness or any other condition. The author’s possible interpretation of what is reported about Plato’s view helps clarify this. In the discussion of the soul, he says that Plato means the eternity of the universal intellect, which is the inner reality of the soul. He says it is untouched by the defects of material things. His phrase “only indirectly” indicates that the soul’s reality is a delicate connection to that source, a flash from it. The beginning of this level of existence is therefore like the beginning of the soul itself, and the body’s readiness is like the readiness of its source. This is the subtle point the author has in mind. — س ره

  103. This later thinker’s argument is confused because it mixes up a shared nature and a general idea in the mind.   117. That is, the kinds would have ceased to remain stable, and then something other than a human might have come from a human, and so on. The argument also leaves out another premise: the kinds are many and distinct, while God is one in every respect, so their differences cannot result from depending on God directly, without intermediaries. The author’s stronger point is not only that the kinds have causes and ends, but that they share the same kind as their Forms. He argues that if the form of a kind were not based on a luminous model, it would be like an individual form produced by chance from matter and its features. Since the human form, for example, is preserved, it must have an eternal model in the creative world. The bodily form is its shadow, and the two are alike in kind. The author sees this problem too: after giving three arguments, he says they do not prove that an intellectual Form belongs to the same kind as its bodily image. God contains all perfections but has no essence of his own.

Knowledge, for example, is a quality in the human mind; the soul’s direct knowledge of itself is a soul-substance; the Intellect’s knowledge of itself is an intellectual substance; and God’s knowledge of Himself is identical with His existence, which has no essence. The concept is the same in each case, but its reality differs. — ط مد

This follows from the fact that possibility, necessity, and impossibility belong to an essence: if one individual of a kind is possible, then all are possible; if one is necessary, all are; and if one is impossible, all are. The author reports this condition in the metaphysics section of this work. He has also used sameness of kind in his earlier argument against chance: wheat does not come from barley.

The fact that a perfection found in one essence exists in another being does not make that other being part of the same kind.   170. Numbers are repetitions of unity. Repeating something is a way for it to appear; if its appearance were separate from it, it would be another thing, not its appearance. Created beings, by contrast, have their own distinct parts: a house is made of a roof and walls, not a roof and another roof. Although unity is the basis of every number, the numbers themselves have different natures, qualities, and effects. Any two different numbers are entirely distinct: two is not three, and three is not two.   178. Here “sameness” means ordinary predication—saying one thing of another—not a definition in which the subject and predicate mean the same thing. — س ره

  179. The commentator is referring to the philosophers’ claim that a shared existence is the main basis for saying one thing of another. They do not mean that predication is the same as judging a statement to be true. A conditional statement, for example, has an “if” part and a “then” part, and the shared existence described here does not make either part a judgment by itself.

    Nor do they mean that shared existence is the only thing needed. Possibility and human nature share an existence; on the accepted view, so do blackness and a body. Yet we do not say “a human is possibility” or “a body is blackness.” We need a link that makes the feature belong to the subject. English shows this link in words such as “possible” and “black.”

    To understand this, we need two distinctions. Something can exist in itself, like a body, or exist as a feature of something else, like blackness in a body. It can also exist for itself or for another. Two natures cannot be joined in every respect, because then they would be one thing, not two. They must differ in one respect and be joined in another. Their difference lies in what each is in itself; their unity lies in one being a feature of the other.

    Take a body and blackness. They share one existence, but the body exists in itself while blackness exists as a feature of the body. The predicate “black” says that the body has that feature. In this way, blackness removes from the body the lack of being black. This is what logicians mean when they say that a statement has two parts: one identifies the thing we are talking about, and the other says what feature belongs to it. At heart, a statement has a subject, a predicate, and a judgment. Any separate link between them belongs to the predicate, not to a fourth part of the statement.

    From this we can see that, in philosophical terms, a statement joins something that exists in itself—the subject—to a feature that exists in it—the predicate. The familiar formula “same in existence, different in meaning” is not quite exact. More precisely, the subject and predicate differ in the way each exists in itself, and they are joined because the predicate exists as a feature of the subject.

    Predication takes different forms according to how the feature belongs to its subject. One form is when a thing is related to itself in the mind, as when we say “a human is a human.” This is an essential definition. Another form joins two levels that differ in completeness, such as a thing and the causes on which it depends. This is called predication between a higher reality and its lower reflection. A third form links a feature to the thing it belongs to, as when we say “the body is black.” This is ordinary predication. Finally, sameness in this sense is not limited to ideas in the mind. A statement that includes a judgment exists in the mind, but the relation between things described here can also hold outside it. — ط مد

  214. The author repeatedly says that the definition of contraries, and some of the rules connected with it, rest on convention. These include the claims that one thing has only one contrary, that contraries must belong to the same nearest general kind, and that substances cannot be contrary to one another. This suggests that he regards only the conditions produced by the division of opposites as essential to the definition. On that account, contraries are two existing, positive things that are not relative to one another and cannot be present in the same subject in the same respect. Anything added to this would rest on convention.

    But it would be very strange to build philosophical conclusions on convention alone. If we add conditions to a definition that follows from a division, we create further possible kinds of opposition. We must either recognize and name these kinds or prove that they cannot exist.

    The usual definition says that contraries are two positive things, neither defined in relation to the other, that take turns in one subject, belong to the same nearest general kind, and differ as far as possible. Here is how its conditions can be understood.

    The first conditions follow from the earlier division of opposites. Either one opposite is the absence of the other, or both are positive. If both are positive, they are either understood through their relation to each other or they are not. The second pair are contraries: two positive things that are not relative terms.

    Why must they have a subject? To call two things opposed, and different from each other in their very nature, we must consider a third thing with which either one can be united. The presence of one then excludes the other from that same third thing. Otherwise, the idea of opposition does no work. Since both contraries are positive, the third thing must be something in which a positive feature can exist. Here subject is used broadly. It may mean the matter that receives a substantial form or the subject that bears an accidental property.

    Yet if we also require the greatest possible difference, substantial forms will not count as contraries. We are left with subjects that bear accidental properties. This is one reason for saying that contraries must be accidents, that they come in pairs, and that the two members take turns in a single subject.

    Why, then, must both belong to one general kind? A substantial form is united in existence with its matter. Together they make one definite thing. If substantial forms could be contraries, that union itself would be enough for each to exclude the other from the matter with which it becomes one.

    An accidental property is different. Its subject can exist without it. The subject and the property do not become a single reality in that same way. Simply saying that the two properties belong to one subject does not explain why one must exclude the other: one accident does not become identical with another merely because they share a subject.

    We therefore need something else with which either contrary can be united so completely that it makes a single kind of thing. In that unity, each excludes the other, because allowing both would amount to making something exclude itself. What meets this description is a general kind, or broader kind, which includes its species. The two contraries must therefore come under one broader kind.

    More precisely, it must be their nearest broader kind. A species is made definite by the distinguishing feature that divides and completes that nearest broader kind. A more distant broader kind does not have the same direct relation to the distinguishing feature. This was explained earlier in the discussion of essence. It follows that genuine contrariety occurs within a kind of accidental property divided into two species, with no third species between them.

    Finally, why must the difference be the greatest possible? Philosophers first recognized opposition in such pairs as black and white. They then found intermediate colors, including yellow and red. These could be called white in comparison with black, or black in comparison with white. They were therefore treated as combinations lying between the two extremes, leaving the extreme ends as the real contraries.

    On this account, the greatest possible difference means that the opposition is not a matter of comparison or changing points of view. The two sides differ in themselves. This last condition makes explicit what their opposition already means. — Ṭ. M.

  241. This suggests that the four familiar kinds of opposition are not a fixed list proved by reason alone; the usual definition of contraries rests on accepted usage.   242. Someone may object: a complete cause must include the absence of anything that blocks the effect. But absence is nothing; how can it help bring something into existence? The effect may depend on something negative, such as the absence of a barrier, but that absence does not bring existence about; the agent does. Or the phrase may mean that each part of the cause is present or absent in the way needed: the agent, matter, form, and a condition contribute by being present; a barrier contributes by being absent; and a preparatory cause may contribute through either its presence or its absence. We may know a positive condition only by noticing that something negative is absent, which can make it seem that the absence itself causes the effect. The same objection and reply apply to the next chapter’s claim that a cause must exist when its effect exists, and that an effect must exist when its complete cause exists. — س ره

  308. They may say that each whole is another existent, but they do not mean that it is a third, single thing counted as one. With a walnut and an almond, for example, the whole is not a third item beside the walnut and the almond, like a pistachio would be. Nor is it a separate arrangement that exists on its own. Instead, it is an existent that is both walnut and almond: one existent is only the walnut, another is only the almond, and a third is the walnut and almond together. This third is “another” because the walnut alone is one, the almond alone is another, and their whole is many things with parts, not one thing.

    This differs from the author’s view. He says that a whole is not a separate existent, because it is many, and existence goes with unity. These thinkers do not accept that existence must mean unity. As Avicenna says, many things can exist as many, even though they are not one. On their view, the repeated parts are clear: if the walnut-and-almond whole is a third thing, as the critic claims, and its arrangement exists only in the mind, then the walnut and almond are repeated inside the three-part whole. They say that number exists in its own right in this sense. The author says that number exists through what the mind draws it from: the units that make it up. Here, “all the units together” means each individual unit; the proponents of a separate whole use the phrase in the way just described.

    One might ask why the author raises the problem of an endless chain at every division, as before. The answer is that his objection is a proof, not just a way of forcing an opponent to accept a consequence. If the two sides of a division were a separate existent and existence necessarily meant unity, there would be another one beyond them. But these thinkers do not accept that existence must mean unity. For them, existence is broader, so the whole can exist as many. A general kind, for example, exists through its many instances. It is distinct from its particular features through its generality, not through another special feature. This point has been explained at length because it is subtle. — س ره

This link between cause and effect is not just an idea in the mind, so it is not enough to say that each is independent of the other in some limited way. The link reflects real degrees of stronger and weaker existence. This argument also rules out a circle of causes. Second, he may mean that such a chain is possible in itself but has not occurred. Third, he may mean that it is possible in reality, which cannot be the point: if it were, the chain of simple beings would not end in basic matter, nor would the higher worlds end in the world of nature.   357. Some thinkers deny that a complete cause comes before its effect because the cause’s matter and form are present with the compound effect and seem to be the effect itself. So the matter and form in the compound do not make the cause and effect identical, as the objection assumes.   359. Philosophers agree that there are four kinds of cause. They argue for goals as causes in their discussion of ends, and for matter and form in their discussion of matter and form. They therefore accuse philosophers of believing in chance, since philosophers say that the world depends on an agent without matter—God. The commentator says the philosophers are right. When physical things interact, their active and receptive effects differ. If fire ignites cotton, the fire contributes one effect and the cotton another. Fire’s effect is already present in it and passes to the cotton, though not like a liquid being poured out. The cotton’s effect is not present before the two meet; it receives that effect from the fire. This is how physical events work in general. Matter can therefore be seen in two ways: as something that has an effect and gives it to something else, or as something that lacks the effect and receives it. The first is an active cause; the second is a receptive cause. — ط مده

He therefore allows some intellects to come from a group of other intellects, and some to come from a whole made up of two aspects, such as two features within the intellects. His view will be explained later. The cause of every affected being has a real unity. One might object that if the simple effect begins to exist after not existing, and if, as already stated, a simple new thing cannot come from a compound, this would lead to an endless chain. The reply is that the Active Intellect is its active cause, the source from which it receives existence: it is one and simple, but it acts under an outside condition, namely a portion of the heavenly motion. The Shaykh’s point is that the active cause cannot itself be compound, a whole made up of two or more things. He says the whole is the cause, not each part on its own, even though the coming together of the parts does not itself exist as a thing. The complete cause of a new event, however, may be compound—for example, something lasting together with a new condition. Other philosophers say the complete cause of a new event is a group of conditions, some of which are absences, such as removing an obstacle or preparing matter. The author has also cited the writer of The Mawāqif, who treats removing an obstacle as the presence of something. A true unity in the world of events, though simple in one respect, may also be compound in another, as the author will explain. — س ره

  393. “Preparer” here is used in its everyday sense, not as a strict technical term. In technical usage, a preparer is something that must first exist and then cease to exist for the effect to occur. A natural philosopher’s agent, by contrast, must exist at the same time as its effect; most people use the word in the same way. For example, when listing the causes of a bed, they call the carpenter its active cause. The carpenter truly is one cause of the bed, alongside the cutting of the wood, the bed’s shape, and its use for sitting. The same applies to a builder and the wood, bricks, and clay that make up a house, its shape, and its use as shelter. Still, these workers are active causes only in the sense used by natural philosophers, who focus on motion and change. They call the cause the source that changes or moves existing matter. The philosopher who asks about existence looks for what gives being: what brings something out of nonexistence, and gives it matter, form, action, and purpose. Since possibility is a negative feature, how can they keep it from sharing in the giving of existence? They can answer that the intellect causes the sphere’s nature, not its existence. The sphere’s existence is made necessary by the intellect, together with its nature and its limited possibility. The intellect, as a light that receives its being from God, gives rise to the next intellect. What is lower comes from what is lower; what is higher comes from what is higher. — س ره

And since existence has different levels, it is fair to speak of agents of existence other than God: these are the different levels of existence. — س ره

  403. More precisely, the First Agent cannot have any extra matter or goal, either in its unqualified action or in its action toward the first effect. Since the same reality gives it both its own being and its power to act, what belongs to it in this respect is not something separate from it. The same applies to the other features. — س ره

  404. The point is that fire burns while it is hot, and the sun gives light while it is moving. Heat and motion may necessarily belong to fire and the sun, but that necessity is not eternal. — س ره

  405. The actions we see in the world fall into two broad groups. In the first, knowledge has no role in producing the action, as with the actions of natural forces. In the second, knowledge does play a role, as when an animal walks. The first group may fit the agent’s nature; this is action by nature. Or it may go against the agent’s nature; this is action by force, as when a heavy body moves upward.

    When an agent’s knowledge helps produce its action, that knowledge is part of the kind of being it is. It allows the agent to recognize what fulfills its nature and to choose it over what does not. An animal seeking food moves toward something it sees. If it finds food, it eats; if it finds a stone, it leaves it. If the animal already knows an action is good for it, it does not need to think further. But if it is unsure, it compares the thing’s features with what would fulfill it. Once it decides the action is good—or decides that it is not—it acts or leaves it alone. This turn toward acting or not acting is what we call choice. Deliberation helps the agent reach a judgment and end its uncertainty. If the judgment is clear from the start, no deliberation is needed. The agent chooses what it already knows to be good, as a speaker says each letter of a sentence without stopping to consider whether to speak each letter or remain silent. As soon as the agent reaches a clear judgment, whether by thinking or without thinking, it acts without delay.

    This shows that voluntary action and compelled action are not two different kinds of action in the world. So we should not divide agents that act with knowledge into those that act by choice and those that act under compulsion, as if their actions worked in completely different ways. A person who compels someone makes one option seem impossible. The person then chooses the other option because they believe it is the only one left. Without the threat, they might have chosen the same option for some other reason. In both cases, the person’s will and choice work in the same way; the difference is in how we describe the situation. In ordinary choice, the person believes they cannot refuse because of some reason they accept. Under compulsion, the reason is a threat or some other pressure that makes refusal seem impossible. For example, someone who moves away from a wall that is about to fall on them acts in the same way as someone who moves because a tyrant threatens to drop the wall on them unless they do. In both cases, the person believes they must move, and that belief leads them to choose the action.

    Society still distinguishes between these cases to protect people and enforce its laws, which bring reward, punishment, praise, and blame. But this is a practical distinction, not a deep difference in how the actions themselves work. Compulsion does not erase the agent’s will; in either case, the action still involves the agent’s will.

    All this concerns agents whose actions depend on the ordinary, mental kind of knowledge. The author also lists two more kinds: acting through satisfaction and acting through providence. He will question the second kind later. Strictly speaking, there are four kinds if we leave aside both compelled action and providence. But the author’s account of God’s knowledge requires another kind. He seems to include it under providence, because the action comes from knowledge alone, without an added motive. The difference is that this knowledge is direct awareness, not a picture or idea in the mind. Some call this way of acting self-disclosure.

    I say: we can sort the kinds of agency by asking first whether the agent knows what it does. If not, its action either fits its nature or goes against it: these are action by nature and action by force. If the agent does know what it does, ask whether the action is chosen. If it is not, the agent acts under compulsion. If it is chosen, ask whether the agent’s knowledge of its action is the same as its action and comes from its knowledge of itself; if so, it acts through satisfaction. Otherwise, the agent knows the action in detail before it happens. If that knowledge is joined to an added motive, the agent acts through intention. If the knowledge itself produces the effect, then either the knowledge is different from the agent’s being, in which case it acts through providence, or it is identical with its being and fully reveals the effect, in which case it acts through self-disclosure. I have also explained this way of dividing the kinds in my poem Gems of Insight. Anyone who wishes to remember it can turn to that poem. — س ره

  406. It is doubtful that acting through providence differs from acting through intention. Fear and shock may hold their attention on the thought of falling, so that no other option remains in their mind; they fall. The person who is used to being there has both options in mind and chooses to stay.   413. Pure potentiality has no feature that distinguishes one kind from another. But first matter is simple, and there is no basis in it for a division into kinds: the general kind would have to include the very feature that distinguishes each kind, while that feature would itself have to be included in the general kind. Such a distinction is hard to make sense of even in things that are fully actual and distinct. It makes even less sense in first matter, which is pure potential. Potentiality, simply as potentiality, has no distinguishing feature, just as nonexistence has none. — س ره

  420. Existence has no parts, and it has no separate instances. What makes its levels different is the same as what they share. But potential existence is still existence when compared with absolute nonexistence, just as a shadow is light when compared with total darkness. The same is true of matter’s love and longing. Someone might say that the love belongs to matter’s existence, not to matter itself. But every possible thing is made of two aspects: its bright aspect, which is its existence, and its dark aspect, which is its nature considered apart from existence. The existence of matter is basic. So it is true to say that matter’s existence loves itself, that it loves form, or that it loves the First Cause through the existence it receives from Him.   421. Matter is the source of longing because it is the potential part of things. Its potential comes from the limitations of souls and natural kinds in the downward order of existence, just as matter’s readiness to receive forms comes from the basic possibility in the Active Intellect. Their changing powers and readiness, and their continuous motions, are their desires and efforts. They are mixed with lack in one way and possession in another because they are joined to matter.

    Without matter, nothing would have the potential to move toward completion, and no action or desire—whether natural or belonging to a soul—could take place. Imagined forms without matter cannot act on one another, mix, join, or rise toward God as earthly matter does. Nor can they move or long for the lasting truth as heavenly matter does. Matter is the source of longing in all who long. How could it have no longing, when it is longing itself? — س ره
