  433. It would be clearer to say that a definition of a human being as a substance that can have dimensions, grow, sense, move by choice, and reason is not adding something outside the thing being defined. Nor is it listing mere conditions or branches. It is listing the parts or levels of the human being when each is considered on its own. When considered together, they form one simple reality. — س ره

    ↩

  434. The movement may have a goal in relation to another movement—for example, Zayd may go from home to a gym to exercise—or in relation to the power of desire, rather than the moving power itself. The moving power’s goal is always the point to which it moves, as with natural movement. Otherwise every movement would be a kind of seeking, whether natural or voluntary, and seeking itself is never the thing sought. — س ره

    ↩

  435. When we consider the active moving power by itself, apart from desire and perception, it is like the natural powers. We may call it the muscular power, or the natural mover found in simple things. In either case, the only thing sought through its movement is the endpoint. — س ره

    ↩

  436. Avicenna also uses “or” here to mean “and.” Otherwise, mere imagination without thought would not differ from aimless action as described by the critics. In this technical sense, aimless action has no rational, thought-based source and so no rational goal. The point reached by the movement—which is always the goal of the active power—is also a goal of imagination and desire. If the active power and imaginative desire do not share the same endpoint, and there is no rational desire, the source of the action must be imagination alone or imagination joined with another source. — س ره

    ↩

  437. I do not like this term. It would be better to call the action a failure in relation to that goal, since what is void does not exist, while this action does. — س ره

    ↩

  438. Democritus held that his tiny bodies shared the same nature, and argued for this from the fact that all bodies have three dimensions. This does not mean that the word “body” is used for several unrelated things, or that one idea points to different real natures. He explained the tiny bodies’ different shapes by denying qualities we feel through touch. He said the tiny bodies in fire are triangles with sharp points that pierce the skin and seem hot; the others are cubes, squares, or spheres, as he thought their simple nature required. He also believed in empty space. All of this is false. — س ره

    ↩

  439. Once the heavenly spheres and planets came together, their positions and rays produced these formations for a purpose. So they did not arise by chance—that is, without an agent, without a goal, or without both. — س ره

    ↩

  440. Empedocles did not claim that the heavenly spheres or the basic elements came about by chance, because he regarded them as brought into being directly. He may have meant that strange features and accidental changes in compound things happen by chance. Some Muslim scholars also called the world of growth and decay “the realm of chance” in this sense. — س ره

    ↩

  441. The mind rejects this claim because “chance” means either that an event has no agent or that it has no goal. Both claims conflict with reality: events have agents and goals. The possibility that something could be otherwise is what makes it need a cause, and a goal is a cause that moves an agent to act. Chance also refers to what is unexpected and rare, while events that happen always or most of the time are not rare. — س ره

    ↩

  442. Necessity rules out chance. No one would say it happened by chance that four is an even number. The material in an embryo’s hand, when it meets every condition for forming an extra finger and the active power acts on it, stands to that extra finger as four stands to evenness. The discussion here concerns goals; the existence of active causes has already been settled elsewhere. It has been shown that when two alternatives are equal, neither occurs until an outside factor tips the balance. At the level of what a thing is, neither of two opposites applies to it. Once causes necessarily bring about their effects, how can the result be by chance? — س ره

    ↩

  443. A Persian couplet says: “Speak of the One; turn from all the rest. Keep one heart, and turn your face toward one goal.” — س ره

    ↩

  444. The words “As for the obstacles” may have been omitted from the original manuscript. The same point applies to obstacles. The author may have thought that the following discussion of withering covered this second case, since obstacles also amount to something missing. — س ره

    ↩

  445. This is the point mentioned earlier: everything has its place in the order of the whole, and the whole order serves as a goal for the causes at its beginning. — س ره

    ↩

  446. If “heavenly arrangements” means physical positions, these are the immediate causes. The deeper causes are the higher souls that move the heavens, especially the sun’s soul, and the higher intellects that guide their movements toward their goals. God encompasses the whole order from beginning to end. Rain is an incidental outcome, not something forced by matter. — س ره

    ↩

  447. The cause that ultimately tips the balance is with God, since He is the true agent. The commentator explained this in the opening of his notes. — س ره

    ↩

  448. This raises an obvious objection: does this not rule out an outcome being favored without a reason, rather than ruling out choice itself? We reply that choosing means one option becomes more likely than another. If one of two equal options becomes more likely because of a further choice, the same question applies to that choice, and the chain goes on forever. If there is no further choice, then one option becomes more likely for no reason. Also, since the goal is what moves an agent to act, without a goal that favors one outcome the agent is not actually acting. To say there is an agent while denying what makes it act is to affirm and deny the same thing. — س ره

    ↩

  449. The theologians say that will stands to power as necessity stands to possibility. They miss that will makes an action necessary only because of a prior motive: the judgment that the action will be useful. Will does not do this by itself. — س ره

    ↩

  450. That is, the two alternatives are equal in reality, and one is singled out only on the opponent’s assumption. — س ره

    ↩

  451. This argument conflicts with the one before it. The first assumes that will is directed toward only one thing; this one assumes that will relates equally to several things. — س ره

    ↩

  452. Here, “rather” corrects what came before; it does not mean “yes.” — س ره

    ↩

  453. If someone asks what tips the balance in favor of this particular motion, the question returns to the second argument. The two points are therefore not separate arguments but one. — س ره

    ↩

  454. As we have learned, each cause has a particular relation to its particular effect. That relation rules out the effect taking a different form. — س ره

    ↩

  455. The commentator says he has not seen the treatise mentioned here. He thinks it may refer to arguments in The Throne of Divine Wisdom and elsewhere: particular features may belong to the identity of an individual thing, even though they are accidental to its general kind. The objections may confuse the individual with the general, or treat what necessarily follows from a thing as if it had to be caused separately. For example, someone might ask why the letter alif is straight and dal is curved, without seeing that an alif without straightness would not be an alif, nor a dal without its curve a dal. These features need no separate cause. If the question is about the letter in general, it has no separate existence; the question comes back to why alif is alif and dal is dal, though what belongs to a thing’s nature needs no cause. This is the point behind the saying that the blessed was blessed from eternity and the wretched was wretched forever. — س ره

    ↩

  456. If someone found two equally strong motives, they would stop and not act. Even a donkey does not move toward water or fodder until it sees them; its desire favors movement over rest only when there is a reason to do so. — س ره

    ↩

  457. Someone might ask how this fits with the sacred saying that God created creation so that He might be known, and the Qur'anic verse “I created jinn and humankind only so that they may worship Me,” which commentators and philosophers explain as “so that they may know Me.” They say that the goal of creation is God Himself. The answer is that His being known is identical with His essence, just as His other attributes are identical with His essence. In another sense, His being known takes the form of a relation to the perfect human being. The goal is direct witnessing: that those who know God know Him through immediate presence, until the knower and the act of knowing no longer remain distinct, as in complete erasure, utter annihilation, and the passing away of annihilation itself. — س ره

    ↩

  458. Some contemporary scholars who follow the traditionist school say that will is an attribute of action and means only willing something other than oneself. The commentator disagrees. The arguments, he says, show that a willer ultimately wills himself: people seek food, drink, clothing, homes, writing, sewing, family, and friends because they seek their own good and love themselves. — س ره

    ↩

  459. In some versions, another line comes first: “I pass by Salma’s home and kiss this wall and that one.” The poet first speaks of the houses generally, then names the particular beloved’s home, as if it stood for them all. A similar couplet says: “I kiss the ground her beauty crossed—what of the house where her beauty dwelled?” — س ره

    ↩

  460. This passage needs some clarification. I will distinguish three points. First, these outcomes are grouped by when they occur in relation to the main goal: before it, as hardness is needed for cutting; alongside it, as a dark color accompanies iron; or after it, as earthly events follow the motion of the spheres. Second, hardness helps cause the cutting, while the dark color merely happens to accompany the iron that is needed. Third, someone might ask how hardness and darkness can be goals if they last as long as the knife does. The reply is that the relevant hardness is the hardness after the iron has been softened and shaped, and the relevant color is the color of the finished knife, not of the iron before it is polished. Another answer is that these qualities may be goals of the powers and natural processes that act on matter and form minerals. Among the names by which God is invoked is: “O You whose treasures are in the mountains.” — س ره

    ↩

  461. The proper goal lies within the hidden side of the world, at the end of the upward sequence of beings, as will be explained in the discussion of the afterlife. The first cause also lies within the hidden side, at the start of the downward sequence. One moves from hiddenness into view; the other moves from view back into hiddenness. — س ره

    ↩

  462. The claim that the defining forms of kinds exist forever rests partly on old assumptions from astronomy and natural science, and partly on the idea that each kind has its own eternal, separate cause. Later work in mathematics and natural science showed those old assumptions to be mistaken. Earlier discussions also questioned whether these separate causes exist. In addition, general rules drawn from nature depend on the conditions we observe now, and we have no proof those conditions will remain the same forever. So we cannot prove that nature must always produce human beings, animals, plants, earth, or the same elements. This differs from the continuing flow of existence as God wills it: that has a complete cause and an unrestricted agent who exists forever and is not limited by conditions or blocked by obstacles. The commentator says the full discussion belongs elsewhere. — ط مده

    ↩

  463. “The first” and “the second” refer to a goal that exists in what receives it and a goal that exists in the agent. — س ره

    ↩

  464. This is true when we look at motion as a kind of change that stands opposite to rest. But when something moves from one place to another, it passes through a series of temporary positions before coming to rest in one fixed place. That final place is the endpoint of the movement. — ط مده

    ↩

  465. Having distinguished good and generosity as terms used for goals, the author now explains what good and generosity mean more broadly. — س ره

    ↩

  466. Suppose an agent performs an action for a goal. If there were no goal, the action would not happen. So the act’s being brought about depends on the goal, just as the agent’s ability to act depends on it. Since the agent acts by its own nature, the goal must be present in some way within that nature, not wholly outside it. The agent has a general, undirected state and a particular state directed toward an action. The action, too, has two levels: the action itself and the fuller state it reaches. A thing can therefore be viewed as the basic fact that it exists and as the fuller state toward which it moves. This is how each created thing has a goal through its cause. What has no further goal and is itself the goal is not made for something else. — ط مده

    ↩

  467. Put another way, in every action the agent seeks itself. For agents that can change, an incomplete self seeks its more complete state, even if it only imagines that state. — س ره

    ↩

  468. The goal that exists in what receives an action, or in someone other than the agent, need not be the final goal. It may be the goal of one action and then serve another goal in a later action, until the chain returns to the agent. For example, a carpenter may make a bed so that a ruler can sit on it. That does not prevent the ruler’s sitting from having its own goal, or the carpenter from also seeking payment or some other benefit that serves his own good. — س ره

    ↩

  469. The author seems to mean that one kind of goal is both a goal and an endpoint in the strict sense. This specific use agrees with the wider, everyday meaning of the word. — س ره

    ↩

  470. Consider their familiar division: “A thing either requires existence through itself, and so is necessary, or it does not.” Yet the Necessary Being is pure, simple existence, standing by itself. His existence does not come from a maker or depend on a subject in which He exists, for He has neither matter nor an essence distinct from existence. So “requires” here means that He does not need another to give Him existence. Similarly, when they say that a substance “stands by itself,” they mean that it does not exist in another thing as an accident does.

    ↩

  471. A final cause is knowledge of the good result of an action. In this case, the ultimate goal is God Himself, so the knowledge in question is God’s knowledge of His own essence and, through it, of all that depends on Him. The philosophers describe this as general knowledge of effects; Mulla Sadra holds that God knows them all in a single, undivided act of knowledge. Since God’s essence is the source of the action, this knowledge gives rise to creation without deliberation.

    ↩

  472. This is natural, created worship: the obedience built into the way each thing is made. It is not the worship required by religious law. The commentator distinguishes commands addressed to people, which leave room for choice, from God’s creative command, through which things and matter take on their nature and powers.

    ↩

  473. The author specifies earthly, animal worship because human worship, considered at that level, is nothing like the worship of the heavenly spheres and their inhabitants. They neither sleep nor grow weary. They worship God without interruption or exhaustion. And what is ordinary human knowledge beside that of the angels who are protected from error, especially those nearest to God? As the verse says:

    Where is the Beloved, and where are you, deceiver? What has the light of eternity to do with those still farther astray?

    But among human beings there is a group superior even to the angels, let alone the heavenly spheres. Of them another verse says:

    Neither the heavens nor the angels possess What lies in the deepest heart of Adam's child.

    These are the finest of God's servants and the choicest beings in creation, especially those who follow Muhammad most completely. It is said of them:

    The Holy Spirit, in the gardens of the highest sanctuary, Has tasted the earliest fruit from our gardens.

    And of their leader it is said:

    If Ahmad were to unfold that majestic wing, Gabriel would remain overwhelmed forever.

    The words of Farīd al-Dīn ʿAṭṭār of Nishapur apply to this whole group:

    My child, day and night these seven turning circles Carry out their work for your sake.

    The worship of the spirits is for you; Paradise and Hell reflect grace and severity toward you.

    The holy ones have all bowed before you; Part and whole are immersed in your existence.

    Do not keep looking down on yourself in contempt; None greater than you is possible in this order.

    Your outward being is a part; inwardly you contain the whole. Even in humility, do not think yourself incapable.

    When the time comes for the whole to rise in rank, The ranks of creation rise through your existence.

    The reason is that a human being who has reached full perfection stands under the Greatest Name, the name Allah. Angels stand under names that express God's freedom from imperfection, such as the All-Holy and the All-Pure. The heavenly spheres stand under such names as the Everlasting, the Exalter, and the Lord. The complete human being knows all the divine names: both those that express God's being beyond comparison and those that describe how His qualities appear in creation.

    Consider the difference. The spirit of a heavenly sphere remains bound to its sphere. But the spirit of a person in this highest human group becomes free—not only from the natural body, but even from the body of the world of images and, beyond that, from both worlds of form. Such a person casts off the two sandals and leaves the two worlds behind. An angel close to God may be a spirit free of bodily limitation, yet still does not possess knowledge of all the divine names in both of these ways.

    These complete human beings bring the rising chain of existence to its highest point. Their intellects have risen beyond the need to use the body and its organs. It is as though they have already taken their bodies off while still wearing them. They stand opposite the pure intellects that mark the beginning of the descending chain. If any veil remains, it will be lifted entirely. This is why ʿAlī said, as his earthly life ended, “By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded!”

    Their worship is therefore nobler in quality than the constant worship of the heavens. A small amount of perfectly sincere action can outweigh an immense quantity of other actions. Their knowledge likewise surpasses the angels' knowledge, because the complete human being knows God through all His names. Perhaps, then, the author's statement concerns human beings simply as earthly human beings, not those who have reached this complete state. — S. R.

    ↩

  474. A thing can be the true goal only through its own independent perfection. Created beings do not exist independently; their existence depends on God. So God is their true goal.

    ↩

  475. More precisely, God is first through His self-subsisting existence and last as the goal toward which we turn. The commentator says that nearness to God means taking on divine qualities; Mulla Sadra calls this resembling the First Principle.

    ↩

  476. This explains why some goals that seem lower than the person can still be pursued. A poor writer seeks payment, which is a better state than being in need. Someone who is generous only in possibility seeks to become generous in action. In general, people seek a fuller state of themselves. The commentator adds that the intention itself is higher than the thing intended, because the intention gives rise to the action.

    ↩

  477. The lower goal exists only in the person’s mistaken picture of it. For example, someone may imagine that giving in to a shameful desire is a sign of greatness. The person thinks their whole self seeks it, but in fact the imagination and bodily appetite seek a passing pleasure.

    ↩

  478. You may object: This answer clearly belongs with the preceding question, not with the present one. I reply: it belongs here too. The present objection was that if a goal makes someone act, and the agent is higher than the result it produces, the agent would have to gain some perfection from a goal beneath it. But the soul, considered in its higher nature, does not perform a particular act to gain a passing, lesser goal; such a goal cannot complete it in that respect. When the soul acts through its connection with matter, however, it can act for a particular goal, because in that respect it can gain what it lacks. If the answer also fits the earlier question, that is no difficulty: the earlier question then has two answers.

    ↩

  479. The commentator says that the world’s true existence depends on God; created things have existence only through Him. In the Persian verse, the word for “or” separates two ideas. It does not show doubt. The heedless may think that some things are enemies and others friends, but all things display the qualities of the true Beloved.

    ↩

  480. God’s knowledge of Himself is active: it brings things into being.

    ↩

  481. An action has a goal in the sense that it reaches a fitting result, the fuller state toward which it tends. God’s own goal, in this sense, is Himself.

    ↩

  482. Harm and loss are called side results because they arise indirectly within the order of material things. God does not directly aim at them.

    ↩

  483. Nature has a kind of prior awareness because a source must in some way hold the basis for what it produces. The power of fire to heat contains the basis of heat; the power of water to cool contains the basis of cold. The result does not come from a source wholly unrelated to it.

    ↩

  484. The commentator reads the Qur'anic verb as “they understand,” so the verse says that people do not understand the praise of other things.

    ↩

  485. The commentator argues that awareness and love appear in every kind of existence, each according to its level. If bodily matter and a higher intellect share the same basic kind of existence, though at very different levels, then even a very faint form of existence has some degree of awareness and love. This is how the author earlier described matter’s natural longing for form.

    ↩

  486. The saying “God is Zayd’s existence” means that God alone has existence in the fullest and independent sense. Created things do not have existence by themselves; God gives them being and holds them in being. There is no second, separate source of existence. The distinction between a thing and its existence points to this dependence; it is not a separate object added in the mind.

    ↩

  487. The claim that orderly action proves planning is not a proof. It may persuade people who do not see how natural results follow from the powers of things. Nature can bring about an ordered result without thinking or choosing it.

    ↩

  488. The two senses are the goal that gives rise to an action and the end at which the action arrives.

    ↩

  489. The commentator explains three connected senses of the world’s final goal: God’s knowledge of the good order before creation; God Himself as the true end of creation; and God as known and met by those who seek Him. The second is the end reached by creation itself; the third is the end as experienced by creatures who come to know God. These differences matter while the seeker and the One sought are viewed as separate. They disappear in complete awareness of God.

    ↩

  490. This refers to both kinds of command: the commands of religious law and the commands built into the way creation works.

    ↩

  491. The commentator says that people attached to worldly things will not be comforted in the next life by imagining those things. When someone loses money or a child, simply imagining them does not ease the grief; it may deepen it. In the next life, people face the real results of their actions: wrongful gain becomes a form of fire, while generosity becomes a good and welcome reality. The next life is the harvest of what people do here.

    ↩

  492. This conclusion is the finest point in this stage, indeed in all these stages. Understanding it joins the book’s ending to its opening and brings the work to completion. It brings together proof and direct spiritual experience—the kind taught by the All-Merciful when joined with awareness of God—as well as reason and transmitted teaching. May God reward the efforts of the one who brought it to completion.

    ↩

  493. An intermediary in existence is one that makes a subject truly have the property it mediates; that property cannot truthfully be denied of the subject. Fire, for example, makes water hot. An intermediary in attribution works differently: the subject is described by association, so the description can truthfully be denied of it. There are several kinds. In the first, the intermediary and the subject exist separately and occupy different places, as with a ship and the passenger it carries when both are called moving. In the second, they exist separately but are not apart in place, as blackness and ebony when we call the ebony black; blackness is what is truly black. In the third, they exist as one, as broader kind and distinguishing feature in a definition, and as essence and existence when we consider what is real. Because an individual plays this third kind of role in the realization of a natural universal, the universal exists only through individuals, not separately from them, as the thinker from Hamadan who lived in Avicenna’s time held. Nor does it exist in a separate world as the archetype of its kind, as some have imagined. Such a creative archetype would itself be an individual of that kind; its greater perfection would not prevent it from sharing its nature with other individuals, just as a perfect human being is still human like an imperfect one. In short, the universal does not act as something that gives existence. It has no existence apart from individuals, and its nature is neither existent nor nonexistent in itself. Existence is neither identical with nor part of it. The universal nature is immersed in the existence of its individual; its real existence is that individual’s own existence. So it is not an intermediary in existence but is attributed to the individual by association. This attribution is metaphorical in ordinary thought, though it counts as demonstrative when seen from a high level of spiritual insight.

    ↩

  494. Scholars disagree about how the parts of a definition, such as a general kind and its distinguishing feature, are joined, although they agree that the mind distinguishes them. One view says that these parts are separate in both essence and existence in the external world. A second says that they are distinct in essence but united in existence, since they are parts that can be predicated of the whole; predication means that they share one existence, while essence is prior to existence in what a thing is. A third view says that they are united in both essence and existence. The author takes a fourth view: these parts have no external reality as separate or unified essences, even though the natural universal exists externally in an incidental way. What exists in itself outside the mind is one simple mode of existence. Depending on its capacities and on which similarities it notices, the mind draws distinct ideas from it. When the author says here and in his other books that the true distinguishing feature is a particular existence, he is expressing this fourth view.

    ↩

  495. “Relation” here means the way God’s existence shines through the world, not a separate relation between two independent things. The commentator distinguishes the world as God’s shadow from the essences where that shadow appears: existence is light, while essences have no independent being. Saying that the world exists through God does not mean God created a second, separate reality. This is why the Qur'anic verse says, “Have you not seen your Lord?” rather than, “Have you not seen your Lord’s shadow?”

    ↩

  496. Every image that appears where the shadow falls is a sign of the original reality from which it spreads. The greater world is like a mirror of God’s high attributes and beautiful names, which are the roots of all things. To know the realities of things is, in the end, to know God and His attributes. This also explains “He taught Adam all the names”: the complete human being knows the realities of the world through God, and this knowledge is itself knowledge of God. Readings of the verse in terms of the realities of the world, God’s attributes, or the names of Muhammad and his family support one another.

    ↩

  497. The commentator says that the verse does not mean God could have held back the shadow but chose not to. God willed the world and brought it about through His generosity and wisdom; all that happens was already known and decreed. The verse uses a conditional form like “If He wills, He can replace you.”

    ↩

  498. “Universal concepts” here explains “natural universals”: an essence considered just as it is, before the mind considers it as universal.

    ↩

  499. The commentator explains the familiar saying that possible essences and fixed entities are not beings in themselves but still have effects. They have no existence of their own; they receive a dependent status when existence gives them its features. This lets us speak of possibility, limitation, and multiplicity without treating these ideas as separate beings. Possibility means that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary for an essence; limitation belongs to essence, not existence; and existence does not multiply by itself, but through the things in which it appears.

    ↩

  500. The comparison shows how concepts such as life, knowledge, and power are drawn from the existence they describe. They are like possible essences drawn from individual beings. The same concept can describe God or an angel, while the relation tells us whether that life or knowledge is eternal or began in time.

    ↩

  501. Every individual fully has the nature of its kind. The universal’s relation to its individuals is like a parent’s relation to children: the whole nature is present in each individual, with that individual’s features making it particular. The nature is not split into parts or multiplied with the individuals; the difference lies in how the mind considers each one.

    ↩

  502. The commentator explains the unity of existence: existence has one shared meaning, and what distinguishes each being is not something added from outside. The same existence appears in different particular forms.

    ↩

  503. The commentator praises the mystery of how God links universal essences with individual existences without a shared part between them. The universal is the particular understood in a different way; the difference lies in how we perceive it. God’s names bring opposites together—the First and the Last, the Visible and the Hidden. The same existence is present in the highest intellects, though it remains free of possibility and change. This is another example of God joining opposites without a common feature between them.

    ↩

  504. In Sufi language, the “secret of destiny” is God’s eternal knowledge of each fixed essence and of the states it will display when it exists. God judges each thing according to what He knows of it. Some say that knowing this secret frees a person from striving and toil. The commentator notes that this is different from the question of why some evils arise in the world.

    ↩

  505. The commentator cites Qur'anic verses saying that good comes from God, while evil comes from oneself; that all things come from God; that people will only will what God wills; and that God erases and confirms what He wills. Here, “from yourself” means “from your own fixed essence.”

    ↩

  506. “Union” here includes all kinds: predication, likeness, sharing a kind, equality, and other forms of sameness, including cases where we do not usually describe them through predication.

    ↩

  507. An effect is not a separate thing alongside its source; it is the source appearing in another way. The commentator says that all created beings depend entirely on God. Their beings, qualities, and actions are links to the One who sustains them; their appearance is held within His appearance.

    ↩

  508. The commentator compares this with the idea that God brings things into being by appearing through them: He reveals them and is hidden in their appearance. At the resurrection, His unity removes their separate forms. This does not mean that God changes His nature or that He has children. It means that created things only seemed to be separate from Him; their reality is His ongoing act, as the Qur'an says, “Each day He is at work.”

    ↩

  509. The objection can be stated in two ways. If the Necessary Being falls under the broad category of relation, it would need a distinguishing feature and would be composite. If it were identical with that broad category, it would be caused by it. The highest category itself is simple, so only the first version leads to composition.

    ↩

  510. You may say that this strengthens the objection: if the Necessary Being is a cause through His very essence, and a cause precisely as cause ... What was intended is that the apparent separation assumed at first is not real. We may affirm causation, but understand it as the unfolding of His acts, not as an independent union of the kind the Muʿtazilite proposes. For God “neither begets nor is begotten”; rather, “Each day He is engaged in a matter.” — س ره

    ↩

  511. If a proof is a judgment of the mind, why does the author say that the mind is not the judge? The commentator answers that he means reason by itself, without God’s light. A proof has authority because it is a light from God. The mind recognizes the truth through a light given to it, just as the saying goes: “Know God through God.”

    ↩

  512. The point is that every category of relation is a kind of essence, but not every identity that depends on a relation belongs to that category. The argument confuses a relation in a thing’s existence with the mind’s separate idea of relation.

    ↩

  513. The commentator objects that the category of relation is still an essence and cannot be drawn from existence alone. A relation in existence, however, is not a quality that rests on a subject; it is the link by which one thing’s existence depends on another. The mind forms the separate idea of relation by considering the two things and the link between them.

    ↩

  514. Relation is a concept formed by thought. It follows the way things exist, but the relation itself is not a separate thing in the external world.

    ↩

  515. The commentator gives two further answers to the problem of time. First, before and after in time are links in existence itself, not the formal category of relation; not every kind of priority or delay belongs to that category. Second, as the Sheikh explains elsewhere, the mind creates the idea of relation. It can consider the earlier and later parts of time together, even though they do not exist together outside the mind.

    ↩

  516. The author offers another answer: time is one continuous reality, not a set of separate pieces. Its parts are joined in one flowing existence. In that way, the earlier and later moments are together in the continuous whole, while each keeps its own place in the sequence.

    ↩

  517. The point is that these things have relational existence, not independent existence, as explained earlier.

    ↩

  518. The alternative would create a circle: possible beings depend on God’s life, knowledge, power, and other perfections. The argument also applies to a possible perfection claimed to belong to God.

    ↩

  519. This note compares the argument with a later proof in the section on divine things. A possible being cannot depend on something impossible in itself. This also answers al-Dawani’s objection to the principle that the noblest possible being must exist: its supposed cause cannot be a perfection in God that is itself impossible.

    ↩

  520. The note cites mystics who say that all things are one reality in different forms. The world’s “attributes” are not qualities added to God; they are features of existence considered in relation to its manifestations.

    ↩

  521. The note lists images that can help explain this relation: a moving flame tracing a circle, motion giving rise to the idea of a path, a flowing present giving rise to time, a mirror and its reflections, and the sea and its waves. It also invokes the Qur'anic image of a lamp within a niche and the sign of unity found in every thing.

    ↩

  522. Ordinary compounds, such as a body made of matter and form, have distinct parts. Numbers, by contrast, consist of repeated ones. The note also compares this kind of predication to statements about possibility or “thingness,” where the predicate is not an added quality in the subject.

    ↩

  523. “Existence without restriction” means existence itself, not a general concept. Its all-pervading reach is an act of the Real, not the Real’s essence considered in itself.

    ↩

  524. The distinction allows two approaches to be reconciled: denying limitations and possible boundaries does not mean denying existence as a positive reality.

    ↩

  525. Eternal necessity means that a thing exists through itself, apart from every distinct external condition or cause.

    ↩

  526. Number offers a comparison: its kinds are simple in meaning, and any distinction between broader kind and defining feature in them is a distinction the mind makes.

    ↩

  527. Fractions belong to the category of relation, not quality, because they are not settled qualities inhering in a subject.

    ↩

  528. This follows one account given by the mystics. Abd al-Razzaq al-Kashani explains the 'Cloud' mentioned in a report about God as the level of absolute oneness, because no one knows that level but God. It is veiled by divine majesty.

    Others take the Cloud to mean the level of unity in which the divine names and attributes appear. A thin cloud hangs between heaven and earth; likewise this level stands between the heaven of undivided oneness and the world of created multiplicity. Kashani rejects this reading of the report. The Prophet was asked where the Lord was before creating the world and answered, 'In a Cloud.' But the level where names and relationships are first distinguished already involves a determination, and Kashani takes everything determined to be created.

    I do not accept that every determination must be created. This is the appearance of God's attributes, not yet His acts in the created world. The fixed realities related to the names and attributes appear as objects of divine knowledge. They are not thereby created things existing independently of that knowledge. Even the first active giving of existence is called the world of command rather than the world of creation in this terminology. On the author's account, the separate intellects belong to the divine realm and endure through God's own enduring reality.

    Moreover, the question concerned the Lord and the level of lordship. That is precisely the level of unity in which the names and attributes are distinguished, as the author states elsewhere.

    ↩

  529. The source seems to omit a second “either.” The note supplies it: existence taken with one attribute is a particular name; with all attributes it is the name “Allah”; with a particular created determination it is a particular possible being; and with all such determinations it is the “Great Human,” the universe as a whole.

    ↩

  530. The note quotes Jami on the fixed entities: before the sea of generosity stirred, they were distinct neither in knowledge nor in external existence; when it stirred, the Necessary and the possible became distinct and the pattern of duality began.

    ↩

  531. By this he means the universal intellect, which embraces the intellects arranged both in higher and lower ranks and alongside one another. It is the enduring reality at the heart of the world. When philosophers say that ‘substance remains,’ substance can mean what everything else depends upon. In this sense the enduring heart of the world is God's abiding face, even as created natures pass and change. It is also the existence that spreads through all things. This reality is later called the ‘Breath of the All-Merciful.’ That name usually refers to the existence that extends through the whole world. It is applied here to the intellect that contains all other intellects because this intellect receives that existence in its fullness.

    It is its first dwelling place, before it divides into many distinct levels—the mother of all places and of the pens. It still remains in the heaven of its own unity. At this level there is no need to treat its essence as something separate from its existence; on the view being defended, intellect has no essence apart from the fact that it exists.

    ↩

  532. God’s self-sustaining power appears at every level: in the concept of substance in the mind, in matter as the subject of material forms, and in the universal intellect as the form of forms and source of all agents.

    ↩

  533. Compound divine names, such as the Living, the Self-Sustaining or the Most High, the Magnificent, can have a unity that produces an effect not found in either name taken by itself.

    An objection: any two names can be put together. What makes this combination a real unity? The answer is that a being must genuinely display both names, either by its created nature or through the qualities it develops. In its created nature, an animal is both hearing and seeing; the heavens display enduring motion and elevation. In conduct, a person may acquire both wisdom and generosity.

    If someone is generous but lacks wisdom, merely calling that person 'the servant of the Generous and Wise' does not bring the two qualities together. In this way, a person who is strongly shaped by one of the divine names may be called its servant even without bearing that name outwardly. The servant of the Guide leads others; the servant of the Giver gives to them.

    As explained earlier, things may appear to a seeker as signs in which the divine names are displayed. From a higher point of view, they may be described as the names expressed in action, because the sign has no independent standing apart from what it displays. At the highest level of sincerity, even the distinction of attributes falls away.

    ↩

  534. The primary names include Living, Knowing, Willing, Powerful, Speaking, Hearing, and Seeing, with “Allah” as their chief. The main names are finite, while their many derivatives are not. “Relation” here includes both pure relations and things described through relations.

    ↩

  535. Once “name” is understood in the mystics’ sense, sayings such as “the world is a manifestation of the names” or “the name is the named” need not be taken as ordinary identity claims. They are the same in existence but distinct in meaning.

    ↩

  536. God's essential names belong to the unseen, and His essence—the hidden treasure—is the unseen beyond every unseen thing. This is one reading of the words, “With Him are the keys of the unseen.”

    Some writers find a symbolic meaning in the letters of the divine name. The letter ha can stand for pure divine identity rather than for an ordinary pronoun. It may be drawn as a circle, with no starting or ending point and with its center equally related to every part of its edge. Some draw two circles instead, to suggest beauty and majesty. The letter waw arises when the sound is extended. Since ha is formed in the throat and waw at the lips, their joining can suggest the divine breath embracing what is hidden and what is outward. The sound is only a sign pointing toward the unlimited divine existence; it does not contain it.

    Alternatively, the 'keys of the unseen' may refer to God's names expressed in action: the intellects through which beings come forth and those through which they return. On either reading, only God knows them fully. Knowledge requires a likeness between the knower and the known. Whatever belongs wholly to the divine realm exists and remains through Him; only He knows its innermost reality.

    ↩

  537. Each divine name has a corresponding fixed entity: the human entity corresponds to the all-gathering name “Allah,” an angel to “the All-Holy,” and an animal to “the Hearing, the Seeing.” These are knowledge-forms that exist with their names, not later effects.

    ↩

  538. The “most holy outpouring” is the essence appearing through names, attributes, and their fixed entities. The “holy outpouring” is its appearance through possible essences in the active world. The first is the self-disclosure of attributes; the second, the self-disclosure of acts.

    ↩

  539. Here “separately” means distinct in essence or concept, not in existence: the names and their corresponding realities share one existence, that of the named. The divine knowledge level is the realm of distinct knowledge, where each thing is known as it is.

    ↩

  540. The note points to Jami and Husayni, who speak of bringing the fixed entities from knowledge into visible reality—from the unseen into direct witness.

    ↩

  541. The mistake comes from confusing a thing's nature with its actual reality. These thinkers hold that existence is fundamental. How, then, could they mean that actual beings are only ideas? The aspect of each thing through which God's action and light appear—His face, power, and will—is not an empty mental invention.

    When mystics say that angels, heavenly spheres, humans, animals, and other creatures are 'considered' or 'conceptual,' they are speaking about the natures of things taken by themselves. Such natures have no independent existence. They are not saying that these beings, as they actually exist, are unreal. The mistake lies in moving from a statement about a nature considered in thought to a statement about a living, existing reality.

    Consider a philosopher who says that a human nature, taken by itself, is equally open to existence and nonexistence. A reader might suppose that an actual human being, while existing, could just as well not exist at that very moment. But while something exists, its existence is certain; it cannot be both itself and not itself in the same respect. Even a thinker who holds that natures are fundamental means the nature as connected with existence, not a bare nature considered in isolation. The poet Shabistari's statement that distinctions are matters of consideration makes the same point.

    ↩

  542. The commentator says the first and second ways of considering a possible being ultimately both concern existence. The first is a general, undivided awareness of its existence; the second considers existence and unity in more detail.

    ↩

  543. An objection: calling Necessary Existence 'existence on condition of absolute freedom' seems to make it existence with a condition attached. Yet the accepted account is that it is existence without conditions. How can both be right?

    The answer is that 'absolute' here means the boundless reach of real existence, not the generality of a concept in the mind. All three expressions used by these thinkers can point to the same pure, simple existence, which excludes nonexistence from itself and is the source of existence for other things.

    'Without condition' means that no limit is imposed on it. 'On condition of being unrestricted' means that unrestricted reality itself; the supposed condition merely says that there is no condition. Even 'on condition of nothing else' can refer to the same reality, because the word 'nothing' removes the limits, natures, and absences we might otherwise add to our thinking. The descriptions differ, but the reality described is one.

    The word 'absolute' will also be used in a different sense: God is true existence, while the existence that flows from His act may also be called 'absolute.' The same word is then used of two different levels, which the author will distinguish later.

    ↩

  544. If reason’s judgments could fail at a level beyond reason, then even the judgment that the world has an eternal Creator could fail. Reason is the highest human power for knowing. Some claims are beyond a limited or confused use of reason, but not beyond sound reason itself.

    ↩

  545. Possible beings need not have independent existence to be real. Their existence may be only dependent and relational: their whole being is need and dependence on the true reality. This does not conflict with unity.

    ↩

  546. The mystic looks beyond the many essences and images that draw attention in different directions to the one existence that gives them life. The note compares this to a mirror and its many reflections: the source remains one while its appearances differ.

    ↩

  547. A human being is only an imperfect comparison for God. A human is limited and made of parts; body and soul are joined in a way that develops the body, but the soul is not its cause in the same sense that God is the cause of all existence.

    ↩

  548. “Balanced” means free from extreme anger, fear, or desire. Such states make the many forms of the imagined world more prominent and distract from the vision of unity.

    ↩

  549. An effect shares the nature of its cause and is not a separate thing beside it; otherwise, it would not truly be an effect. In this account, existence itself is God’s power. All sources of action are levels of that power, while actions considered apart from their existence are like mirages.

    ↩

  550. The note reads “the world is God’s book” as an image of creation as writing: intellects are complete words, souls are names, changing natural forms are actions, and accidents are like grammar and marks in writing. The world’s many forms are written by one author.

    ↩

  551. The note quotes a mystic who says he is like someone who has seen a dream but cannot speak of it, while the world cannot hear. He cannot put the secret into words, and most people cannot receive it.

    ↩

  552. The objection has two possible targets. If it concerns Unity (wahidiyya), that level includes many names, attributes, and fixed entities. If it concerns Oneness (ahadiyya), there are no names or distinctions there, and so no duties or created beings. Multiplicity, duties, and actions appear at later levels. The unity described here is the unity that gathers many things together.

    ↩

  553. The author calls the third level “universal,” but it is not a general idea shared by many things. The commentator notes that “universal” can mean a natural kind, a rule that applies to a whole class, or a word such as “a man.” The author uses the term loosely because this level is long to explain and easy to confuse with the abstract idea of existence.

    ↩

  554. Philosophers often use “numerical unity” to mean that something is one individual. They also sometimes use it for the kind of oneness found within numbers, which the mystics take as a sign of the special unity of God.

    ↩

  555. “Timeless” here means without beginning in time, not uncreated in essence. The all-pervading existence is described as the Throne of the All-Merciful, a created reality, and an extended shadow.

    ↩

  556. All-pervading existence differs from basic matter and a general kind. It is fully real and includes all beings. Matter and a general kind, by contrast, are only potential and vague until they appear in particular forms. One is full and complete; the others are marked by lack.

    ↩

  557. The author makes this distinction because readers often mistake “absolute existence” for the simple mental idea of existence. The same words can refer either to that idea or to the real existence that appears through beings.

    ↩

  558. This note refers to philosophers who say that essences are real in themselves and that existence is only a mental idea.

    ↩

  559. The mystics call all-pervading existence “matter” by comparison. They do not mean that it is material or something that can be received by a subject. It is higher than both matter and receptivity.

    ↩

  560. The note links the name “Breath of the All-Merciful” with sayings attributed to the Imams, who used “dust” or “matter” for this all-pervading existence.

    ↩

  561. The note explains why al-Qunawi calls this existence “general.” In other fields of study, “general” can be a figure of speech for what is broadest and first noticed by the mind. The Real is the first reality and the most evident at every level.

    ↩

  562. The fixed identities of possible beings have no independent existence, though their features and effects depend on all-pervading existence. “No existence” here means no separate, self-standing existence. The note contrasts God’s complete independence with the possible beings’ total dependence.

    ↩

  563. The commentator stresses how closely the levels of existence are related. Even restricted existence, represented by the Universal Intellect, belongs to the divine realm in a deeper sense. All-pervading existence, whose first manifestation is the First Intellect, belongs to that realm even more fully. It is the source of all that comes into being; the reverse is not true.

    ↩

  564. All-pervading existence is not a separate product made by God. It is God's own act of flowing forth and appearing; nothing stands apart from Him as a second source. In thought, the First Intellect is the first distinct being to proceed from God, though it is preceded by the act of proceeding itself. This does not limit God's power or suggest that He hands creation over to another. All lower acts and beings are contained within this one act, especially in all-pervading existence. Its appearance is God's own self-disclosure, not something separate from Him; the First Intellect is the active expression of His power and continues to exist through Him.

    ↩

  565. The word “existence” may be used for God if it means real existence as it applies to its source, not merely as an abstract idea in the mind. In that case, the word points to the reality that gives rise to the idea. This is the existence that rules out nonexistence.

    ↩

  566. Rumi's “nothings” means the natures or identities of created things, not their real existence. The mystics sometimes call a nature “nothing” because, on its own, it is neither existence nor nonexistence. It appears to exist when joined with existence, but it does not exist independently. This is not the claim that a particular person is God. For the mystics, existence is primary and has different levels: one level is cause, another effect. The created nature is dependent on existence and is only an aspect of what appears. In this sense, God is the root of our being, and we are wholly dependent on Him.

    ↩

  567. Some theologians allow “existing” as a description of God but not as one of His names. The dispute concerns how the word is used.

    ↩

  568. A real thing is either existence itself or a particular nature. A nature, considered on its own, is neither necessary in existence nor necessary in nonexistence, so it cannot be the Necessary Being, who is pure reality and existence. God is not the abstract idea of existence, but the reality that makes existence known. Those who deny any shared meaning between God's existence and the existence of created things to avoid likening God to creation go too far: every act of knowing depends on God's light, and every being appears through Him.

    ↩

  569. The commentator's objection is verbal rather than a real disagreement. He distinguishes true existence, all-pervading existence, and restricted existence, but also explains that all-pervading existence is God's manifestation, while God is hidden through the intensity of His manifestation. A manifestation is not separate from what it manifests. There is one reality with different levels, not a second or third God. None of these levels implies that God enters created things, becomes joined to them, or takes on their defects. Restricted existence is connected to a created nature only in the sense that the nature describes it.

    ↩

  570. At the inward level, the scriptures do not differ in their central teachings. All things are signs of the One who has no equal, and each reveals God's oneness and unity. God's words in the world and in the soul do not run out or change; His light does not fade, and His giving does not cease. What belongs to God is timeless, while matter and nature are changing and passing away. The mystics also distinguish three levels of unity: knowing about a fire from its light, seeing the fire itself, and being consumed by it. In the last two, the one who knows is lost in the simple, all-pervading reality.

    ↩

  571. “Turn toward” means that they earnestly seek this unity. For most people, it can be reached only through spiritual discipline and moral fairness: treating others as oneself and preferring their good to one's own until the sense of separation falls away. Not reaching this deepest experience does not invalidate a person's direct or reasoned knowledge of unity.

    ↩

  572. The wording means that the signs or descriptions point toward the same thing, even if the words differ.

    ↩

  573. As long as there is someone pointing and something being pointed to, there are still two. True unity cannot be captured by that kind of description. This is why Ali speaks of “lifting the veils of majesty without a gesture of pointing.”

    ↩

  574. A real nature, such as humanity, can exist both in the world and in the mind. Abstract ideas such as existence, nonexistence, possibility, and thingness cannot exist as separate things in the world. But the mind does not invent them from nothing. It forms them by reflecting on other ideas. So real natures are drawn from things that exist; abstract ideas are drawn from the mind's ideas about those things.

    ↩

  575. A particular nature, such as humanity, is a basic idea that can refer to a real person. Ideas such as possibility and thingness are formed by thinking about those basic ideas. They do not point to a separate object in the world. The same word “thing” may also be used for the nature itself, but that does not give it an independent existence.

    ↩

  576. The first appearance of existence is one with the later appearances. The sense of many separate acts comes from the many forms that reflect it, not from any division or repetition in the source or in its act. Once we set aside the many mirrors, there is no second source or repeated act.

    ↩

  577. Some sayings from the Imams identify the “Face” that remains after all things perish with the Imam himself. This does not conflict with the author’s use of “Face” for all-pervading existence. The note says that the Muhammadan and Alawite realities are one light in the realm of spiritual authority.

    ↩

  578. The note explains how scripture can speak of God's “hand,” coming, or sitting without treating Him as a body. Such words refer to His acts and their effects, which are His way of appearing, not to body parts or qualities added to His essence. The perfect human being, who acts through God rather than through an independent self, can be called God's hand or eye. The same is true of the powers of intellects and souls. All these are expressions of one divine power, not separate parts of God.

    ↩

  579. The “point of direct insight” means hearing the speaker within the words. Al-Sadiq is said to have repeated a verse until he heard it from the One who speaks it. This is why some mystics prefer reciting the Qur'an to many prayers: in reciting it, they feel that they speak God's words on His behalf.

    ↩

  580. The commentator says the mistaken Sufis accept unity within the many forms of the world, but deny that multiplicity can also be gathered within God's unity. The complete view includes both: God's hidden oneness and His appearance through many forms. This is more complete than treating God as only the sum of the world. All serious thinkers agree that God's essence cannot be fully known. It is the unbounded reality of existence, not the limited form of a “Great Human” or any other created being. If this divine reality did not exist, there would be no reason for the agreement the author describes.

    ↩

  581. The commentator reads the opening words as “while they think this,” signaling that the claim he describes is false.

    ↩

  582. These disputes arise because “existence” has several meanings: God's true existence, all-pervading existence, and the general idea of existence that the mind applies to particular things. When the mystics say that God is beyond existence, they mean He is beyond created, limited existence or the mind's abstract idea of existence. They do not mean that God is beyond reality itself. Denying one limited sense of existence does not deny existence in every sense.

    ↩

  583. “True existence” can mean God, who exists through Himself and for Himself. It can also mean real existence, as opposed to an abstract idea in the mind. Here it has the second meaning. The claim is obvious and easily stated, yet important enough to remember constantly: we need to see existence flowing through all things before we can call even a rose or a thorn a manifestation of God.

    ↩

  584. The phrase “fixed identities” may sound as if the natures are separate from existence, and it may sound like the Muʿtazilite teaching. But the two views differ. For the mystics, fixed identities depend on God's knowledge and are never separate from it. The Muʿtazilites treated them as independent of every kind of existence, both in the world and in knowledge.

    ↩

  585. The author grants that a nature must be able to receive existence, but it need not already exist in order to do so. Its natural readiness is enough. He adds that possible beings may have earlier forms in nature or in God's knowledge, before their later forms appear in the world.

  586. God's existence is simple and complete, yet it contains every level of existence. In that sense, His knowledge is one and undivided, while also knowing every being and nature in detail. His names and qualities include the fixed identities that belong to the beings He knows.

    ↩

  587. “Time” here means a level or stage, not ordinary time. The verse's denial that the human being was a “thing” refers to a particular existence in the physical world, while its affirmation of humanity refers to the nature. The saying about God and nothing being with Him concerns the same distinction. There is no contradiction.

    ↩

  588. The note compares natures to basic matter in a compound thing. Matter is where imbalance and weakness appear, which keeps these defects from being attributed to God. This does not mean God fails to give what He can; it means that the nature of what receives existence also shapes what it can receive.

    ↩

  589. The fixed identities can be seen as a display of God's hidden name, because they are known within His hidden unity before they appear in the world.

  590. Indeed, most minds trained in reasoning—perhaps all—find this bewildering. What makes a nature the nature it is does not exclude nonexistence, light, or darkness. It is therefore unlike pure existence or pure light. How, then, could such natures be God’s own states when He is sheer manifestation and actuality, especially since the natures are not themselves created separately? Some investigators, however, approach the question from unity: if natures can in some sense be called things, they say that everything called a thing belongs to His states. They distinguish leaving existence out of consideration from treating nonexistence as a feature. Earlier in the book we quoted the view that natures are existences to which particular forms of existence are attached. There is also this consideration: natures are forms known to God, and His knowledge is His attribute.

    ↩

  591. The wording from al-Qunawi is unclear on its own and does not prove the author's point. The commentator says there may be more in the surrounding passage that would make the meaning clear, but he does not have it at hand.

    ↩

  592. The word “knowledge” may seem unnecessary here, since the note is discussing what appears to things. But the author includes it because in divine knowledge, knower and known are one.

    ↩

  593. A feature belongs to something only under certain conditions. For example, an intellect has a certain level of existence when it is separate from matter, while a plant grows only in a suitable place and season. A quality that belongs to something under one condition does not automatically belong to it—or cease to belong to it—when that condition changes. Existence appears in endlessly many ways, even though its basic patterns are limited.

    ↩

  594. The note alludes to Qur'an 13:17: water flows through valleys according to their measure, while foam washes away. Here, existence is like the water, and natures or particular determinations are like the foam carried on it. What makes a thing appear is existence; its nature shapes the form that appearance takes.

    ↩

  595. Natures differ partly through their own character: just as the maker does not make blackness black or whiteness white, their difference is not something separately added to them. Their differences also reflect the order of the most holy outpouring. The different levels of existence mirror one another: differences in the natural world reflect differences in the imaginal world, which in turn reflect differences in the higher spiritual and divine levels, ultimately corresponding to God's names and qualities. These names and qualities are not caused by anything beyond God. As a saying in Nahj al-Balāgha puts it, “Whoever asks ‘Why?’ has made Him subject to a cause.”

    ↩

  596. Defects and blameworthy features include both limits recognized by reason and faults defined by religious law. A thing’s limits belong to it insofar as it is a bounded nature. Its existence and its luminous aspect, by contrast, come from existence and from the face of God.
